paper_title: Beyond the Estimate: Wiener-Informed Decoding for Easier Training of Pixel-Space Flow Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Learning velocity fields directly in pixel space is difficult and slow. We show that coarse second-order image statistics can ease this task: frozen Wiener estimates improve velocity learning, with gains extending beyond the linear predictions they explicitly provide. Moreover, we observe similar but complementary gains from frozen bases and pixel decoding. These observations motivate Wiener-informed Decoding (WiD), which uses statistical knowledge both for direct prediction and to organize decoder computation without modifying native blocks. WiD combines a trainable Wiener prediction path with coefficient interfaces that inject features into the native decoder and return its predicted coefficient corrections, with these components initialized with data statistics. All introduced parameters, including the spectrum and coordinate transforms, are trained jointly under the original pixel-space velocity objective. Across model scales and decoder architectures, WiD accelerates training and improves generation quality with modest parameter overhead. It also yields smoother gradient trajectories and remains effective with representation alignment. WiD improves class-conditional and text-to-image generation across different resolutions. On ImageNet 256 x 256, PixelDiT-XL with WiD reaches FID 1.53 after 500 epochs, achieving comparable quality to PixelDiT with 37.5% fewer training epochs. Statistical denoisers contribute beyond the estimate: their computational structure can also ease pixel-space training.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Pixel-space flow models offer simpler generative pipeline, but not an easier learning problem. By operating directly in pixel space, they remove the need for separate, pretrained autoencoder. However, the denoising network must operate on noisy high-dimensional pixels while learning natural image structure, which makes optimization slow and challenging (Li & He, 2026; Ma et al., 2026). Recent work addresses the challenge in two prominent directions. (i) Prediction-space approaches seek more learnable target parameterizations, such as clean-image prediction (Li & He, 2026) and rank-asymmetric velocity prediction (Chen et al., 2026a). (ii) Architectural approaches distribute contextual modeling and dense pixel prediction across specialized components. For example, DeCo (Ma et al., 2026) and PixelDiT (Yu et al., 2026) pair contextual backbone with fine-grained pixel decoder. These advances make pixel generation more tractable by changing the parameterization or computational organizationand motivate closer look at the pixel denoising task itself. However, high dimensionality does not imply an absence of exploitable structure. Natural images often possess correlations across space and color, whereas the added Gaussian noise is isotropic. The second-order statistics yield closed-form linear denoiserthe Wiener estimator (Wiener, 1949; Kailath et al., 2000). Although this estimator cannot capture the full complexity of natural images, it helps previous studies (Wang & Vastola, 2024; Lukoianov et al., 2025) investigate the learned denoising behavior and locality. Motivated by these observations, we ask training question: is it possible to ease pixel-space velocity learning by explicitly providing this statistical estimate? Observation: fixed estimate already makes substantial difference. We construct fixed Wiener estimator from statistics to provide an analytic velocity base and train the DiT (Peebles & Xie, 2023) 1 Preprint NUS HPC-AI Lab (a) Analytic bases rescue direct velocity prediction DiT in pixel space. (b) Analytic bases yield competitive quality under native recipes. (c) WiD provides stronger and more persistent gains on PixelDiT. Figure 1: Analytic Wiener bases ease pixel-space velocity learning. We train B-size models for 40 epochs on ImageNet 256256 w/o REPA and report FID-10K results w/o CFG. (a) With the same DiT-B/16 setup, adding DCT or PCA Wiener base rescues the velocity prediction baseline. (b) DiTs with analytic bases reach the performance range of several pixel-space methods. Each method (c) When added to native PixelDiT, our Wieneruses its native training and evaluation recipe. informed Decoding provides stronger and more sustainable gains than frozen Wiener bases. to predict the residual correction under the velocity objective. We consider two typical constructions: global DCT (Ahmed et al., 1974) for image-wide spectral structure and patch PCA (Zhang et al., 2010) for local spatial feature. Both analytic bases rescue the otherwise struggling plain DiT (Figure 1a), bringing generation quality into the range of contemporary approaches (Figure 1b). Consequently, even coarse statistical knowledge can ease the burden of velocity learning. frozen statistical prediction is not the whole story. For DiT, our diagnostics further show that much of the reduction in velocity prediction error lies beyond the fitted linear component (Figure 2a). Thus, the effect of Wiener bases is not confined to correcting linear prediction. This leads us to consider the computation behind the estimate: the Wiener estimator transforms noisy observation into statistical coordinates, adjusts its coefficients according to the noise level, and maps them back to pixels. Can we go step further and use these operations to organize the denoisers computation, rather than only adding the resulting estimate to its output? Pixel decoding provides natural and task-aligned interface for this integration. In PixelDiT and DeCo, the backbone provides semantic context, while the decoder maps noisy pixels to velocity the same inputoutput task addressed by the Wiener estimator. We observe similar but complementary gains from frozen Wiener bases and pixel decoding (Figure 2b). Our input-perturbation tests support the task alignment: the direct pixel pathway shows closer Wiener alignment than the semantic pathway (Figure 2c). Therefore, we incorporate the estimators analysis and synthesis operations into the pixel decoder as trainable components, while retaining the semantic backbone architecture. Approach: from frozen bases to adaptive decoding. We introduce Wiener-informed Decoding (WiD) that incorporates statistical knowledge in two ways. (i) statistical starting point. Using patch PCA statistics, we initialize direct prediction path to produce the Wiener velocity estimate. It turns noisy patches into statistical coordinates, scales their coefficients according to the noise level, and maps them back to pixels. (ii) Coordinates for decoder computation. We also allow noisy-patch coordinates to integrate with the decoders native input embeddings as additional features. Alongside its original pixel-space velocity output, the decoder also predicts correction to the coefficient-space estimate. The sum of the Wiener-branch and pixel-head predictions is supervised by the original training objective, and introduced parameters are trained jointly with the network. WiD improves training stability and efficiency, and accommodates different pixel-decoder architectures with modest parameter increase. Empirically, it reaches comparable generation quality in fewer training steps, with gains that persist further into training than frozen bases (Figure 1c). We validate WiD on class-conditional and text-to-image generation tasks across different resolutions. Contribution Summary. We summarize our contributions as follows. Observation. We show that coarse statistical estimates can ease pixel-space velocity learning, with error reductions beyond the fitted linear responses. The observation motivates us to use the computation behind the estimate, rather than only its output. Preprint NUS HPC-AI Lab Method. We introduce Wiener-informed Decoding (WiD), which integrates trainable statistical prediction path with coefficient-based feature processing and output correction. Results. We demonstrate improved training stability, efficiency and generation-quality gains across different pixel-decoder architectures with modest overhead.

sections.title: 3.2 BEYOND THE ADDITIVE LINEAR PREDICTION
sections.content: An analytic base supplies prediction that the network would otherwise have to learn. But does it also help the network learn the remaining prediction? We investigate this by comparing the velocity predictions with well-trained reference model: the official PixelDiT-XL checkpoint at 320 epoch. At each fixed t, we fit an affine prediction ℓf from zt to each models complete velocity output , and similarly fit ℓref to the reference fref . For PCA, the fit is shared patch-affine map; for DCT, it includes independent RGB-affine maps at each frequency. Each affine family contains the corresponding frozen Wiener base as zero-bias special case, and subtracting the fitted response removes its explicit additive contribution. We measure errors in decomposed parts: Elin(f ) = 1 Eℓf ℓref 2, Erem(f ) = 1 E(f ℓf ) (fref ℓref )2. (9) We fit by least squares on 4,096 validation images and score on 3,072 disjoint images with two fixed noise draws each. Figure 2a reports the reduction in each error while applying Wiener bases to DiT, averaged over five time points. We observe that the remaining prediction contributes most of the improvement, and that the linear-error reduction shrinks with training. These results suggest that frozen base does more than provide better starting prediction: it may also help the network organize its computation to learn the remaining prediction more effectively. 4 Preprint NUS HPC-AI Lab

sections.title: 3.3 PIXEL DECODING AND STATISTICAL PREDICTION
sections.content: Pixel decoding organizes velocity learning by separating contextual modeling from dense pixel prediction. We examine its effect using the same reference and patch-affine decomposition as above. Relative to plain DiT, native PixelDiTs improvement also lies primarily in the remaining prediction (Figure 2b). However, these gains do not make the statistical estimate redundant. Adding frozen PCA base to PixelDiT further reduces both the fitted linear error and the remaining error. These additional gains generally narrow over training, paralleling the trend in FID gains in Figure 1c. We next compare the responses of native PixelDiTs two input pathways with those of the Wiener estimator. With and fixed, we compute each pathways Jacobianvector product (JVP) for the same isotropic unit perturbation δ to zt. The interface in equation 6 gives jpix = (ztD)δ, jctx = (sD)(ztB)δ. (10) The first holds the contextual features fixed; the second holds the decoders direct pixel input fixed. We compare these output-velocity JVPs with the Wiener responses At( (cid:102)M )δ, after removing each responses component parallel to δ. Cosine similarities are averaged over 256 held-out images and {0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9}. On average, the direct pixel pathway is more aligned with both statistical references than the contextual pathway, and the gap widens over training (Figure 2c). Together, these observations motivate us to integrate the statistical estimator into pixel decoding. (i) Frozen bases and native pixel decoding both improve the remaining prediction, yet their combination yields further gains, showing similar but also complementary benefits. (ii) The direct pixel pathways closer alignment with Wiener responses supports the decoder as natural interface for this integration. To pursue more persistent gains, we make the estimators prediction path and coordinate transforms trainable parts of the decoder, allowing them to evolve with learning (Section 4).

sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 5.1 CLASS-TO-IMAGE GENERATION Setup. We choose PixelDiT-XL/16(Yu et al., 2026) as the backbone to evaluate our Wiener-informed Decoding on class-conditional ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009) generation. Following its original training recipe, we use AdamW optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2015; Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) with the learning rate of 1e-4 for the first 160 epochs, and then step down to 1e-5 on ImageNet 256 256. For ImageNet 512512, we fine-tune the 260-epoch 256256 checkpoint for 50 epochs. The global batch size of 256 and REPA using DINOv2-B (Oquab et al., 2024) with weight 0.5 remain the same. As is stated in Section 3.1, we use 51,200 images (about 4% of the training set) to compute the spatial patch statistics to initialize WiD. The computation costs us only 1 minute with one GPU and 12 CPU DataLoader workers, which we consider quite practical in large-scale training scenarios. We generate 50K samples from EMA weights using 100-step FlowDPMSolver (Xie et al., 2024) and classifier-free guidance (CFG) (Ho & Salimans, 2021) with interval (Kynkaanniemi et al., 2024), and report FID (Heusel et al., 2017), sFID (Nash et al., 2021), IS (Salimans et al., 2016), precision, and recall (Kynkaanniemi et al., 2019) using the ADM evaluation suite (Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021). 7 Preprint NUS HPC-AI Lab Table 2: Class-conditional generation on ImageNet 512 512. Wiener estimation has long history in image denoising and restoration (Wiener, 1949). Methods such as BLS-GSM (Portilla et al., 2003) and NLBayes (Lebrun et al., 2013) build on Wiener estimation using statistics for image denoising. Similar to statistical operations in our WiD, BM3D (Dabov et al., 2007) organizes computation by constructing representations, applying empirical Wiener filtering to coefficients, and reconstructing the 9 Preprint NUS HPC-AI Lab image through inverse transforms. Furthermore, Deep Wiener Deconvolution (Dong et al., 2020) has proposed to integrate Wiener operations into learnable feature-processing pipeline for image deblurring. Together, these studies show how statistical priors can be constructed and utilized. Statistical structure in diffusion. In studies of diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021), statistical estimates also provide way to understand learned denoisers. Linear fits reveal Gaussian structure associated with generalization (Li et al., 2024), while Gaussian score approximations capture moderate and high noise-level behavior and help accelerate sampling (Wang & Vastola, 2024). Data statistics can also explain locality patterns otherwise attributed to architecture (Lukoianov et al., 2025). These findings connect classical estimation to modern generative models, and inspire us to explore using statistical priors in generative learning. From estimation to generative learning. Motivated by these insights, our research takes step further to study how this statistical knowledge can aid pixel-space velocity learning: WiD uses the statistics to initialize the prediction path as structured starting point, and integrates the computational operations and coordinates into the decoder.

sections.title: 6.2 PIXEL-SPACE FLOW MODELS
sections.content: Prediction parameterization. Recent approaches ease pixel-space learning by changing what the network predicts. JiT (Li & He, 2026) predicts clean images, while AsymFlow (Chen et al., 2026a) combines full-rank data prediction with low-rank noise prediction to reconstruct the velocity. Recently, k-Diff (Jin & Wang, 2026) learns scalar that controls the datanoise mixture predicted by the network, while retaining velocity-space supervision. simplified linear analysis motivates this parameterization by relating the preferred mixture to data dimensionality. Separately, WiD aims to address the similar learning difficulty within velocity prediction. Pixel decoding. Another direction is to separate contextual modeling from dense pixel prediction. PixNerd (Wang et al., 2026a) uses patch-wise neural fields, PixelDiT (Yu et al., 2026) uses pixel transformers, and DeCo (Ma et al., 2026) uses context-conditioned MLP decoders to alleviate the learning difficulty. WiD builds on this separation: it retains the native backbone and decoder blocks in PixelDiT and DeCo, adding statistical interfaces around their existing computation. Connection to preconditioning. Preconditioning addresses differences in scale and geometry that can hinder diffusion and flow training. EDM (Karras et al., 2022) normalizes network inputs and residual targets using noise-dependent scaling and skip connection. Preconditioned Flow Matching (Ahamed et al., 2026) instead uses reversible data transformations to improve the conditioning of intermediate flow distributions. WiD is related in the use of statistical structure to ease learning, but focuses on decoder design: trainable Wiener prediction path interacts with the native decoder.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present Wiener-informed Decoding (WiD) to improve the velocity learning of pixel-space flow models. Specifically, we have shown that coarse second-order statistics can ease pixel-space training, and the gains from frozen Wiener bases extend beyond their explicit linear predictions. Motivated by these insights, we developed WiD, which combines trainable statistical prediction path with coefficient interfaces that connect it to the native pixel decoder. We demonstrate that WiD enhances training efficiency and stability while consistently improving generation quality across model scales and decoder architectures, benefiting both class-conditional and text-to-image generation with modest parameter overhead. These findings suggest that statistical denoisers can contribute beyond the estimate: the computational organization is also helpful for learning pixel-space generation. sections.content: A.1 DECODER STRUCTURES IN PIXELDIT AND DECO (a) Decoder structure of PixelDiT. (b) Decoder structure of DeCo. Figure 5: Illustration of decoder structures in PixelDiT and DeCo. In this work, we use two representative pixel decoders from PixelDiT (Yu et al., 2026) and DeCo (Ma et al., 2026) to validate our Wiener-informed Decoding approach. As shown in Figure 5, both decoders process the noisy input zt, use the contextual features from the backbone to compute scale, shift and gate for pixel-wise modulation, and finally project normalized features to the velocity vθ. Specifically, PixelDiT decoder involves Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) and Feed-Forward Network (FFN) (Vaswani et al., 2017) blocks, while DeCo decoder mainly uses MLP layers. Input initialization for WiD on DeCo. The initialization in Section 4.2 preserves each decoders native positional encoding. PixelDiT adds global positional embeddings after projecting RGB values, whereas DeCo jointly projects RGB values and patch-local cosine positional features. For pixel in patch i, DeCos original embedding can be written as E0zt,i,q +Eposϕ(q)+b, where E0 contains the RGB columns of the joint projection and positional information ϕ(q) is shared across patches. We initialize its RGB projection and the coefficient expander in WiD as [E0, Epos] (cid:55) [ 1 2 E0, Epos], WF = 1 2 L(E0)U0, (15) leaving the bias unchanged. With the full-rank orthogonal basis U0, the injected coefficients recover the other half of the RGB contribution, as in equation 14. The summed features therefore match the original embedding before entering native DeCo decoder blocks at the initial state. Output initialization and normalization for decoders with WiD. Both architectures zeroinitialize the coefficient-correction and native pixel-output projections, including their biases. Output normalization follows the native decoder: in DeCo, both heads receive features from its existing per-pixel, non-affine LayerNorm (Ba et al., 2016); in PixelDiT, the coefficient head uses per-pixel RMSNorm (Zhang & Sennrich, 2019), matching the native output heads normalization. 15 Preprint NUS HPC-AI Lab A.2 ADDITIONAL IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS Table 6: Detailed settings of the five model configurations used in this work. On ImageNet 256 256, we sample 50K images using FlowDPMSolver-100 with the same seed 1600 as the official setting of PixelDiT-XL/16, and use the same ADM evaluation protocal to compute the scores. On ImageNet 512512, we follow the seed 10000 of the official setting of PixelDiT. Therefore, the results are reproducible with our open-source code and checkpoints. Computational overhead. On PixelDiT-XL/16, WiD increases the denoiser parameter count from 797.38M to 804.86M and the analytical forward cost from 311.19 to approximately 315.32 GFLOPs, corresponding to increases of 0.94% and 1.33%, respectively. sections.title: B ADDITIONAL DIAGNOSTIC DETAILS
sections.content: We expand the five-time averages in Figure 2. The analyses below are mainly about frozen Wiener bases and native pixel decoding, before introducing adaptive WiD. B.1 COMPARISON OF PREDICTION ERRORS Evaluation protocol. We use the official PixelDiT-XL epoch-320 EMA checkpoint as the prediction reference and evaluate B-size models at 10, 20, 30 and 40 training epochs. sections.title: C LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: In this work, we mainly focus on easing velocity learning for pixel-space image generation tasks. Actually, we think the perspective of statistical denoising may also be helpful for other flow generative models. Therefore, explorations of integrating statistical denoisers into other generative tasks are also attractive directions, such as latent space generation, and language, audio, as well as video generation. In the future, we are planning to improve upon our current approach, and take step further to explore the potential of integrating Wiener-informed structures directly into diffusion transformers, and try to develop next foundation architecture for flow-matching tasks. 19 Preprint NUS HPC-AI Lab
